name: U.S. History
fwnote: Codes are the Illinois Learning Standards for Social Science for grades 6-8 (inquiry, civics, economics, geography and history); the suffixes LC, MdC and MC mark less, moderately and more complex expectations. The alignment was made by the course author and is not a certification by any agency.

1.bq: How did the meeting of the Americas, Europe and Africa change the lives of all three peoples?
std: SS.G.2.6-8.MdC
Compare and contrast how places and regions differ in their cultures and physical environments
SS.G.3.6-8.MdC
Explain how changes in transportation and communication link settlements and spread ideas and culture
Explain the several causes behind historical events and the range of effects those events produced
SS.H.2.6-8.MdC
Examine the many factors that shaped how people saw their world in a given era
SS.H.3.6-8.MdC
Spot gaps and limits in the historical record by comparing different kinds of sources
1.write: Who gained and who lost the most when the Americas, Europe and Africa met after 1492? Write an argument that answers this question, using at least three pieces of evidence from the unit.
rooms: The World Before 1500 — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: How did people in the Americas, Europe and Africa build such different ways of life before their worlds met?
ch.talk: Many people in Illinois have never heard of Cahokia. Why do you think a city this important was left out of so many history books?

l.look: What can the spear point tell us that the story cannot? What can the story tell us that the spear point cannot?
List one advantage and one problem of each way of life. Which would you choose, and why?
Why do you think corn is at the center of this Maya creation story? What does it tell you about how important farming was to the Maya?
What surprised the Spanish soldiers? What does this tell you about how Europeans expected the Americas to look?
How did roads, runners and quipus solve problems that other empires solved with writing and wheels?
Which choice would you make first, and why? How does this show the ways people adapt to their environment?
What can you conclude about this town from these objects? What else would you want to find out?
What does burying weapons under the tree stand for? Why do you think the eagle was placed at the top?
Choose one need. Explain how each environment shaped the way people met that need.
Which two events happened only one year apart? What does this list show about what was happening in different parts of the world at the same time?

l.t: New Tools and a Divided Church
l.look: What is Luther complaining about? Why might poor people in Europe have agreed with him?
Why would giving away huge amounts of gold make gold worth less? What impression do you think Mansa Musa wanted to leave?

ch.bq: What happened when the peoples of Europe, Africa and the Americas met, and who gained or lost the most?
ch.talk: The Pueblo towns spoke different languages and had their own leaders. Why was uniting them both so hard and so important?

l.look: Would you sign up? Explain what might push someone to take such a dangerous trip.
What did Columbus notice about the Taino? What do his words suggest about his plans for them?
Does signing a treaty give a nation the right to rule people who never agreed to it? Explain your thinking.
How did the Aztec writers see the Spanish? Why is it important to read accounts from both sides of a conquest?
Rank these reasons for the Spanish victory from most to least important: weapons and horses, disease, civil war, the capture of Atahualpa. Explain your top choice.
Pick one food or animal that crossed the ocean. Explain how its journey changed people's lives, for better or worse.
Why would a Spanish priest criticize his own country so strongly? Who do you think he wanted to read his book?
Were these voyages failures or successes? Use one explorer as an example to explain your answer.
Why might each side think it got the better deal? What long-term problems could this trade cause for Native communities?
Why would Elizabeth mention that she is a woman in a speech to soldiers? How did she try to inspire them?
Which place received the most enslaved Africans? About how many times more went to Brazil than to North America?
What details does Equiano give about the ship? Why was his book, written by someone who lived through the Middle Passage, so powerful for readers?

2.bq: How did the English colonies grow and change between 1585 and 1763, and who gained and who lost as they did?
std: SS.G.2.6-8.MdC
Compare and contrast how places and regions differ in their cultures and physical environments
SS.EC.1.6-8.LC
Explain how choices about money and resources affect the welfare of individuals, businesses and society
SS.CV.2.6-8.LC
Describe where constitutions, laws, treaties and international agreements come from, what they are for, and their effects
SS.H.1.6-8.MdC
Connect specific events and developments to the wider historical context around them
SS.H.2.6-8.MdC
Examine the many factors that shaped how people saw their world in a given era
2.write: By 1763, many colonists said they enjoyed the rights of English subjects. Did life in the thirteen colonies match that claim? Write an argument that answers this question, using at least three pieces of evidence from the unit.

ch.bq: Why did people come to the English colonies, and how did their arrival change life for the people already living there?
ch.talk: If you had been a Roanoke colonist when John White sailed away, what would you have done to survive, and whose help would you have needed?

l.look: Why do you think Smith made this rule? Why might some of the gentlemen colonists have been angry about it?
Would you sign? Give one reason for signing and one reason against it.
How does Rolfe describe the Africans who arrived? What does his short, plain report leave out about their lives?
What two things did the signers promise to do? Why might this matter for a group that had no charter?
What did Winthrop mean by comparing the colony to a city upon a hill? How might this idea shape the way Puritans treated people who disagreed?
Why did Williams think forcing people's religion was wrong? Why would Puritan leaders see this idea as a threat?
What choices did Metacom have? What might have happened with each one?
What does this scene tell you about why New Amsterdam grew, and why England wanted it?
What promises did Penn make in this letter? Why might Lenape leaders have been hopeful, and why might they have been careful?
About how many times larger was the colonial population in 1700 than in 1650? Who is not counted in these numbers?
Why did the trustees make these rules, and why did settlers want them changed? Whose voices are missing from this debate?

ch.bq: How did the English colonies build their own ways of working, believing and governing by 1763, and who was left out?
ch.talk: How did the fur trade help both Native nations and Europeans, and how did it harm them?

l.t: New England: Sea and Town Meeting
l.look: How would you vote, and why? Who was left out of this decision, and does that matter?

l.t: The Middle Colonies: Grain and Many Peoples
l.look: About how many times larger was the colonial population in 1760 than in 1700? Name two reasons the colonies grew so fast.

l.t: The Southern Colonies: Tobacco, Rice and Indigo
l.look: Why might planters have wanted workers from rice-growing regions? What does this tell us about who built South Carolina's wealth?
Who made money at each step of this voyage, and who paid the price?

l.t: The Middle Passage and Enslaved Lives
l.look: What details show the suffering of the Middle Passage? Why are first-person accounts like this one important?
What do these reactions tell you about what white colonists feared? What did they choose not to do?
What values do these sayings teach? Why might these ideas appeal to colonists trying to build new lives?
How did Edwards try to move his listeners? Why might a sermon like this draw such strong reactions?
Which of these rights would later appear in American founding documents? Why would colonists care so much about the first one?
What message did Franklin want to send with this cartoon? Why might a cut-up snake be a good symbol for the colonies?
Why did the same peace treaty look so different to these two people?

3.bq: How did the American colonies become one nation, and how well did the new nation live up to its promise of liberty?
std: Explain the several causes behind historical events and the range of effects those events produced
SS.CV.4.6-8.MdC
Analyze the ideas and principles in the U.S. founding documents and how they shape the political system
SS.CV.2.6-8.MdC
Explain how government began, what it does and how it is organized, drawing on the U.S. and Illinois constitutions
SS.CV.1.6-8.MC
Judge the powers and duties of citizens, political parties, interest groups and the news media
Ask questions about individuals and groups to explain why they and their achievements matter historically
Identify sources that represent multiple points of view to help organize a research plan
3.write: Between 1763 and 1791, Americans fought for liberty and built a new government. Was the American Revolution a true revolution for all Americans, or mainly for some? Write an argument using at least three pieces of evidence from this unit.
rooms: How a bill becomes a law

ch.bq: How did loyal British colonists become people ready to fight for independence?
ch.talk: Paul Revere is famous, but many riders spread the alarm that night. Why do you think some people become famous in history while others are forgotten?
ch.story: Two Lanterns and a Fast Horse

l.look: How much did the colonial population grow between 1740 and 1770? Why would a fast-growing population make a line on the map hard to enforce?
Which argument do you find stronger, and why? What is one thing both people might agree on?
How does this message show loyalty to Britain and protest at the same time?
How can what people buy, or refuse to buy, be a form of political action? Can you think of an example today?
Why might Revere have shown the event the way he did? How can a picture be powerful even when it is not fully accurate?
Would you buy the cheaper tea? Explain why a low price did not end the protest.
Why did punishing one colony make the other colonies feel more connected to it?

l.t: The Shot Heard Round the World
l.look: Emerson wrote this more than 60 years after the battle. Why might he call it the shot “heard round the world”?
Why would Congress ask for peace and build an army at the same time?
What does Paine mean by calling government a “necessary evil”? Why might this idea appeal to colonists in 1776?
Put this sentence in your own words. Which idea in it do you think is most important, and why?
Can a document be important even if the people who wrote it did not live up to it? Explain your thinking.

ch.bq: How did a new nation with a small, poorly supplied army defeat the most powerful empire in the world?
ch.talk: Many soldiers could have gone home that winter, but most stayed. What do you think kept them at Valley Forge?
ch.story: A Winter of Huts and Hunger

s.t: A Divided People Goes to War

l.look: Who really came out ahead at Bunker Hill? Use details to support your answer.
What would you advise your nation to do? What risks come with each choice?
Who are the “summer soldier” and the “sunshine patriot”? How was Paine trying to affect his readers?
Why might a country wait to see who is winning before joining a war? What did Saratoga prove?
Does it matter why an ally helps you, as long as it helps? Explain your thinking.

l.t: War on the Sea and in Illinois
l.look: Why might French settlers in Kaskaskia have been willing to accept Clark without a fight?
What is Abigail Adams asking for? Why might the Revolution have made her think about women's rights?

l.t: African Americans and the Fight for Freedom
l.look: Whom did this offer include, and whom did it leave out? Why would Britain make this offer?
How can an army lose battles and still win a war? Use Greene's strategy to explain.
Why do you think the treaty lists each state by name? What does it mean to be “sovereign”?
What pattern do you see between northern and southern states? What does this suggest about how the Revolution changed slavery?

ch.bq: How did Americans create a government strong enough to work but limited enough to protect their liberty?
ch.talk: The delegates met in secret. Was that a good idea for writing a plan of government for a free people? Why or why not?
ch.story: A Hot Summer Behind Closed Doors

l.look: What are the risks of a leader with too much power? What problems might come from a leader with too little power?
According to this article, who holds most of the power: the states or the national government? What problems could that cause?
What does this article forbid? How might this rule have shaped the future of Illinois?
What would happen to this club over time? How is it like the government under the Articles?
How were Shays's rebels like the Patriots of 1775? How were they different?

l.t: Two Plans for a New Government
l.look: Which idea of fairness do you agree with more? Is there a way to honor both?
Under the Great Compromise, which of these states gains more power in the House, and which gains more in the Senate? Explain.
About what fraction of the population was enslaved? Why did the way enslaved people were counted matter so much to both North and South?
Why might delegates design an office differently if they already trust the first person who will hold it? What risk does that create for the future?
Pick two goals from the Preamble and explain them in your own words. Why does it begin with “We the People”?
What is Madison saying about human nature? How do checks and balances answer his concern?
List the five freedoms in the First Amendment. Which one do you think matters most in your life, and why?

4.bq: As the young United States grew stronger and larger, who gained, who paid the price, and what began to divide the nation?
std: SS.CV.2.6-8.MC
Analyze what governments, officials and bureaucracies at various levels can and cannot do
SS.CV.1.6-8.MC
Judge the powers and duties of citizens, political parties, interest groups and the news media
Explain the several causes behind historical events and the range of effects those events produced
SS.G.3.6-8.MdC
Explain how changes in transportation and communication link settlements and spread ideas and culture
SS.EC.1.6-8.LC
Explain how choices about money and resources affect the welfare of individuals, businesses and society
Sort historical events and developments into examples of change and of continuity
4.write: Between 1789 and 1844, did the United States become more united or more divided? Write an argument that answers this question, using at least three pieces of evidence from the unit.
rooms: Civics · The Three Branches — test prep

ch.t: Growing Pains in the New Republic
ch.bq: How did the first leaders turn the words of the Constitution into a working government, and what did they argue about?
ch.talk: Why do you think Mount Vernon now teaches visitors about the enslaved people who lived there, and not only about George Washington?
ch.story: Mount Vernon: Two Stories on One Hill

l.look: Which side would you choose, and why might a title matter more than it seems?
What are the benefits and risks of a leader choosing advisers who disagree with each other?
About what fraction of the people counted were enslaved? Which group of people is missing from this table?
Why did Hamilton connect paying debts to liberty and trust?
How could Hamilton and Jefferson read these same words and reach opposite answers about the bank?
What is each person worried about? Is there a way both concerns could be addressed?
Which party would each person probably join? Explain using what each party stood for.
Why would this family cheer for Pinckney's Treaty?
Why might the U.S. government have wanted this small spot of land? What did it later become?
Why might a young, weak nation want to avoid permanent alliances?

l.t: President Adams and the XYZ Affair
l.look: If you were President Adams, would you choose war or peace talks? Explain what you would gain and risk.
"Abridging" means cutting short or limiting. Why did critics say the Sedition Act went against these words?

ch.bq: How did the young United States grow and test its strength, at home and against more powerful nations?
ch.talk: The Corps depended on help from Native nations and from Sacagawea and York. Why do you think their part of the story was often left out of older history books?

l.look: "Brethren" means brothers. What was Jefferson trying to tell Americans after such an angry election?
What are the trade-offs when a government cuts taxes and shrinks its army and navy?
"Province" here means area of responsibility. Put Marshall's sentence into your own words.
Why would Jefferson call whoever owned New Orleans an enemy, even a friendly country?
Clark spelled "ocean" his own way. What feelings does this short journal entry show after 18 months of travel?
How can one explorer's report shape what a whole nation believes about a place? Whose knowledge was missing from Pike's view?
Would you have kept paying tribute or sent the navy? Give one reason for each choice.
By about how much did exports drop from 1807 to 1808? What does the 1809 number suggest happened after the embargo ended?
How was Tecumseh's idea about land different from how the U.S. government made treaties?

l.t: The War Hawks Get Their War
l.look: Why would news of Perry's victory matter so much to Americans after the early losses in the war?
Why was the sight of the flag at dawn so important to Key? What did it tell him?
If the treaty was already signed, did the Battle of New Orleans still matter? Explain your thinking.

ch.bq: How did new machines, new roads and waterways, and the spread of cotton pull the nation together and push it apart?
ch.talk: The steamboat brought good things to some people and terrible things to others. How can one invention have such different effects on different people?

l.look: Was Slater a hero, a thief, or something else? Explain how your answer might depend on where you lived.
Write two or three sentences you might put in a letter home. What would you say is good and bad about mill life?

l.t: The National Road and the Steamboat
l.look: Who do you think should pay for a road that crosses several states? Give a reason.
In which ten years did New York City grow the most? How might the Erie Canal, which opened in 1825, explain it?
About how many times more track was there in 1860 than in 1840? What might explain such fast growth?
How did the number of enslaved people change after the cotton gin was invented? What connects these two facts?

l.t: The Slave Trade Inside the Nation
l.look: Explain how the ban on the Atlantic trade and the spread of cotton together caused the domestic slave trade to grow. Who paid the price?
Douglass wrote this about learning to read as an enslaved boy. Why were slaveholders so afraid of enslaved people learning to read?
Why might a plan meant to unite the regions end up causing arguments between them?
Notice the words "brought into" and "from now on." How did this wording leave room for some people to stay in bondage?
Why would Jefferson compare the Missouri debate to a fire alarm in the middle of the night?
"Henceforth" means from now on. What was Monroe telling Europe, in plain words?

5.bq: As the United States grew bigger and more democratic, whose freedom grew and whose was taken away?
std: Use maps and other geographic representations to explain how places and regions relate to changes in their environments
Explain the several causes behind historical events and the range of effects those events produced
Explain how and why people's viewpoints have shifted across time
SS.CV.3.6-8.LC
Compare the methods people and groups use to change society, advance the common good and defend rights
SS.CV.2.6-8.LC
Describe where constitutions, laws, treaties and international agreements come from, what they are for, and their effects
5.write: Between 1821 and 1860, the United States grew larger and, for some people, more democratic. Did freedom grow for most Americans in these years, or mainly for some? Write an argument that answers this question using evidence from at least three chapters of this unit.

ch.bq: When more people gained a voice in government, why did others lose their rights and their homes?
ch.talk: Sequoyah's syllabary helped the Cherokee govern themselves, but it did not stop the loss of their land. What does that tell you about power in the 1830s?

l.look: There were 261 electoral votes, so a winner needed 131. How many more votes did Jackson need?
Would you call this town a democracy? Explain your answer using at least two of the people described.
What might go right or wrong if the mayor gives the job to the campaign manager? How is this like the spoils system?
Webster says liberty and union cannot be separated. How does this answer Calhoun's idea of nullification?
Who does Jackson say is misusing the government? Why might this message be popular with ordinary voters?
The law uses the word “choose.” Based on the reading, did Native nations really get to choose? Explain.
What does Marshall say about Georgia's laws? Why did this ruling still fail to protect the Cherokee?
What choices, if any, did these families have? What does this scene tell you about who held power during removal?
How could two people see the same event so differently? What would each want a newspaper to say about it?

s.t: Hard Times and a New Party

l.look: What would you do, and why? How could many people making the same choice make a panic worse?
Is it fair for a campaign to build an image that is not fully true? How do campaigns today try to shape how voters see a candidate?

ch.bq: How did the United States grow to reach the Pacific, and who gained and who lost as it did?
ch.talk: Who do you think benefited most from the growth of San Francisco, and who paid the highest price? Use details from the story.
ch.story: From Sleepy Village to Gold-Rush City

l.look: O'Sullivan says the continent was “allotted by Providence,” meaning given by God. Whose point of view is missing from this idea?
Would you take the job? How did the knowledge of mountain men help open the West to settlers?
What would you leave behind? Why did many families abandon belongings along the trail?
Why might a family choose the long, risky journey? What does this tell you about religious freedom in the 1840s?

s.t: Texas and the War With Mexico

l.look: Why might a Tejano join a revolt against Mexico? What risks did Tejanos face whichever side they chose?
Travis wrote this as he asked for help. Why do you think his letter became famous after the Alamo fell?
Why might Polk compromise with Britain but take a harder line with Mexico? What does this suggest about his goals?
Grant fought in this war as a young officer. Why might his view be important? Why might he have felt differently years later?
About how many times larger was California's counted population in 1860 than in 1850? What caused this growth?
Compare this promise with what happened to many Californios. Why might a promise on paper not be kept?

ch.bq: How did newcomers and reformers change what it meant to be American before the Civil War?
ch.talk: Why do you think the Underground Railroad used secret code words? What does its story tell you about who led the fight against slavery?
ch.story: Roads to Freedom in the Dark

l.look: In which decade did immigration grow the most? What events in Europe help explain the jump?
What is each man afraid of? Are there any ways their interests are actually the same?
About how many times larger was Chicago in 1860 than in 1840? What helped it grow so fast?

l.t: Revival and the Push for Change
l.look: What are some ways she could work for change without voting? Which ways do people still use today?
Why did Dix describe the conditions in such strong detail? What did she want the lawmakers to do?
What does Thoreau mean by living “deliberately”? Why might he think living simply would help him do that?
“Equivocate” means to avoid giving a clear answer. What is Garrison promising his readers?
Why would the Fourth of July feel different to an enslaved person? What point is Douglass making to his audience?
Why were so few records kept? How can a historian decide which stories to trust?
How might working for abolition have changed the way she saw her own rights? Explain the connection.
Compare this line with the Declaration of Independence. What small change did Stanton make, and why is it a big idea?

6.bq: How did the Civil War and Reconstruction change what freedom and citizenship meant in the United States?
std: Explain the several causes behind historical events and the range of effects those events produced
SS.H.1.6-8.MdC
Connect specific events and developments to the wider historical context around them
SS.CV.2.6-8.LC
Describe where constitutions, laws, treaties and international agreements come from, what they are for, and their effects
Analyze how the outlook of source creators shaped what the historical record contains
Organize relevant evidence into a coherent, well-supported argument about the past
SS.CV.4.6-8.MdC
Analyze the ideas and principles in the U.S. founding documents and how they shape the political system
6.write: Was the Civil War a “new birth of freedom,” as Lincoln hoped? Write an argument that answers this question using evidence from the war and from Reconstruction. Explain what changed for Black Americans and what did not.
rooms: The Road to War & Freedom — test prep
Reconstruction to the Present — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: Why did compromise over slavery keep failing until the nation split apart?
ch.talk: Why do you think thousands of ordinary people traveled so far to listen to three hours of political arguing?

l.t: A Question from the Mexican War
l.look: How could both farmers feel they were being treated unfairly? Why was this so hard to solve?
About how many times larger was the enslaved population in 1860 than in 1800? Why would this growth make slavery harder to end?

l.t: A Law That Angered the North
l.look: Which part of this law do you think made Northerners who did not care much about slavery suddenly angry? Explain.
Are there some questions that should not be decided by a simple vote? Use this example to explain your answer.
What does it tell you about the country when the same event is reported so differently in two regions?
Why might it be dangerous for a country when a major political party is popular in only one region?

s.t: A Court, a Debate, a Raid

l.look: Taney claimed he was describing how people thought when the Constitution was written. Why do you think his words made so many people angry in 1857?
What is the “house” in Lincoln’s speech? What did he predict would happen to it?
Can a person be fighting for a just cause and still use methods that are wrong? Explain using John Brown as your example.
Douglas came in second in the popular vote but last in electoral votes. How could that happen?
According to this document, what was the main issue that led South Carolina to secede?
Who was Lincoln speaking to here? What was he hoping they would do?

ch.bq: Why did a war that many expected to end in months become a long and bloody struggle?
ch.talk: Why might a soldier’s letter tell us things about the war that a general’s official report would leave out?

l.look: Why did Lincoln think the whole world was watching the American Civil War?
The Confederacy did not let enslaved people serve as soldiers for most of the war. How does that change the comparison of possible soldiers?
What loyalty mattered most to Lee? How was his choice different from the choice made by people in western Virginia?
What does this tell you about what Americans expected war to be like in 1861? How did their thinking change?
If you were in charge of a navy anywhere in the world in 1862, what would you do after hearing this news? Why?
Why do you think letters and mail from home mattered so much to soldiers living this way?
About how many Union soldiers died of disease for every one who died from battle? What does that tell you about camp life?
How might women’s work during the war have changed what people believed women could do?
What did Grant mean by “move immediately upon your works”? What kind of leader does this message show?
What are the strengths and dangers of each kind of general? Which kind do you think the Union needed, and why?
How might seeing photographs change the way people at home felt about the war?

ch.bq: How did the Civil War change from a fight to save the Union into a fight for freedom?
ch.talk: The attack on Fort Wagner failed. Why is it still remembered as an important moment in American history?

l.look: When Lincoln wrote this, he had already drafted a plan to free enslaved people. Why might he have described his goal this way in public?
Which enslaved people did these words cover? Which did they leave out?
According to Douglass, what would Black men win for themselves by serving in the army?
Why did many people call these draft rules unfair? How could the rules have been made fairer?
How would inflation like this affect the South’s people and its ability to keep fighting?
Was the Union right to stop the exchanges? Think about the soldiers in the camps and the Black soldiers who might be left behind.
Why did holding the high ground give the Union army such an advantage? How did this help decide the battle?
“Four score and seven” means 87. Count back 87 years from 1863. What event was Lincoln pointing to, and why?
How do you think Northerners and Southerners each felt that July? Why did these two events together matter so much?
Is it fair to target an enemy’s supplies and property in war, even if ordinary people suffer? Give reasons for your view.
How did Grant’s terms at Appomattox match the spirit of Lincoln’s words?
The U.S. population in 1860 was about 31 million. About what share of all Americans died as soldiers? Why might newer estimates be higher?

ch.bq: What did freedom mean after slavery ended, and why were so many of Reconstruction’s promises broken?
ch.talk: Why do you think learning to read was one of the very first things so many freedpeople wanted after slavery ended?

l.look: Which argument do you find stronger? What could a plan include to address both worries?
How were these rules similar to slavery? How were they different?
Tennessee was readmitted first, before the Reconstruction Acts. Why do you think most states did not return until 1868 or 1870?
Should a president be removed for political disagreements, or only for serious crimes? Explain how the Constitution’s checks and balances apply.
Which earlier Supreme Court decision did the first sentence overturn? Why was that important?
“Previous condition of servitude” means having once been enslaved. Who does this amendment protect? Who is still left out?
Washington was a boy when slavery ended. What does his short sentence tell you about how freedpeople felt about education?
How would owning land have changed life for freed families? Why do you think the government did not give it to them?
Why was it so hard for sharecroppers to get out of debt? What could have helped them?
What is the difference between having a right on paper and being able to use it? What does a government need to do to protect rights?
Was the Compromise of 1877 a good solution? Who gained from it and who lost?

l.t: Jim Crow and the New South
l.look: Was Reconstruction a success, a failure, or both? Use at least two facts from this chapter to support your answer.

7.bq: How did growth in the West, in industry and overseas change who Americans were, and who paid the price for that growth?

Compare the methods people and groups use to change society, advance the common good and defend rights

Examine the many factors that shaped how people saw their world in a given era

7.write: Between 1860 and 1920, the United States grew in land, industry and power. Was this growth good for all Americans? Write an argument that answers the question, using evidence about at least three different groups from this unit.
rooms: Reconstruction to the Present — cards, quiz and lab

ch.bq: Who gained and who lost as the United States spread across the West after the Civil War?
ch.talk: Why do you think it took so long for people to try to save the bison? Who worked to bring them back, and why?

l.look: Which person do you think had a better chance of making money? Explain why.
In which ten years did the miles of track grow the most? What might have caused that?
Why does it matter whether the stories we tell about the past include everyone who was there?
